title: You are the Christ (Mark 8:27–30)
hook: at Caesarea Philippi, Peter says it: you are the Messiah, the anointed one
carry: who do you say I am?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a blind man at Bethsaida saw men like trees, walking, and then every man clearly. Your line was sight comes in stages.

Someone new starts at work, and before anyone really knows them, the theories begin. He's the one who used to be at that other place. She's like the last manager, only quieter. Now, on a road far in the north, near the towns of Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks his friends a simple question: "Whom do men say that I am?" They have the talk ready. Some say John the Baptist. Some say Elijah. Some say one of the prophets. Then he turns the question around, and there's nowhere to hide: "But whom say ye that I am?" And Peter answers.
screen: `A ROAD FAR IN THE NORTH.` → `WHOM DO MEN SAY THAT I AM?` → `BUT WHOM SAY YE?`

segments.voice: Peter says four words in the old King James Bible: "Thou art the Christ." Christ is not Jesus's last name. There was no Mr. and Mrs. Christ. It's a title. The Greek word is Christos, and it means the anointed one. It translates a Hebrew word, mashiach, which comes into English as Messiah. Anointed means oil poured on your head. In the Hebrew Bible, the prophet Samuel pours oil on young David to mark him as king, and priests were anointed too. In Jesus's day there were Jews who hoped for an anointed one, a king from David's family. When Peter says Christ, he's saying: you are that one. Back in the storm on the lake, the disciples asked, what manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? Now someone finally says it out loud. Mark's very first line had already told the reader: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." The disciples just took half the book to catch up. Then the strange part: Jesus charges them to tell no one. Scholars still argue about why, and Mark never fully explains. One hint comes in the very next scene: the word Christ meant something different to Peter than it would turn out to mean. Christians confess it in their creeds: Jesus is the Christ. But notice how he asked. Not what do people say. What do you say.
screen: `WHOM SAY YE THAT I AM?` · `CHRIST IS A TITLE, NOT A SURNAME.` · `ANOINTED: OIL ON A KING'S HEAD.` · `HIS ORDER: TELL NO ONE.` · then, large: `THOU ART THE CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Maybe you pray to Jesus every day, maybe you're learning about him for someone you love, maybe you honestly don't know; imagine the road, and the question turned toward you: who do you say I am? Don't reach for the right answer, or the answer your family gives; find your own word, even if it's teacher, or stranger, or I'm not sure yet. If you pray, you can simply say what you find, and just be honest.
Christ. From the Greek Christos, the anointed one, the same word as the Hebrew Messiah. A title, not a surname.
Your line: who do you say I am? Peter answered in four words. One hundred ninety-three days now.

howItsDone: Christians confess Jesus as the Christ, and in churches that use the Creeds, the congregation says it aloud in worship; some Christians use Peter's question as a regular prompt for personal prayer.

fork.setup: you're Peter, on the road near Caesarea Philippi. he looks at you and asks: but who do you say I am?
fork.reveal: Peter says "Thou art the Christ." and then, surprisingly, Jesus tells them all to keep it quiet.

original.note: Greek: anointed, from chriō, to rub with oil. it translates the Hebrew mashiach.

trapdoor: what you thought: Christ was Jesus's last name.
what it means: a title. Peter names him the anointed one, the Messiah some hoped for.
what a scholar hears: Christos translates mashiach. and Jesus's order to tell no one is part of what scholars call Mark's messianic secret.
recall: what's handed on from one hand to the next

notes: Caesarea Philippi placed 'near the springs where the Jordan begins' (Banias, at the foot of Mount Hermon). Confirm the phrasing.
'Almost exactly the middle of Mark' is a common structural observation (8:27–30 as the hinge of the gospel). Confirm.
Messianic secret: the term is associated with William Wrede's 1901 study; the trapdoor says 'scholars since 1901'. Confirm.
Pronunciation given as khree-STOS (Koine); some teach KHRIS-tos. Keeper to choose.
